column1: # English forms, to tell which word an example sentence shows.
# A Spanish form can belong to two words ("vino" is wine, and "he came"):
# the sentence goes to the one whose gloss its English translation uses. A
# regular form is recognised by its ending ("dogs", "boxes", "walked",
# "making", "stopped", "tried", "quickly"). The forms that can't be are
#   - irregular ones ("came", "children"), and every form of a word of two
#   - the forms in -er and -est, regular or not ("bigger", "easiest",
#   - the past of a verb in -ee ("agreed"): so do "seed" and "feed".
# A gloss word matches each of its forms and the base it is a form of ("come"
# and "came" match each other); two forms of one base don't match each other
# base<TAB>form,form,...   Lowercase words without spaces. A form may stand
# under two bases ("better"). The build stops on a malformed row or a base
# A base is a word of its own: it is never taken for a regular form of a
# shorter word ("early" is not "ear" with -ly). The last section lists words
# for that reason alone. So a regular form must not be made a base: with a
# line for "building", "is building" would no longer show "to build".
# Not here on purpose: the negatives of "do" ("don't" would show hacer in
# every negative sentence) and a line for "not" (it would give "nos", the
# plural of "no", every sentence with "nos" and a negative).
